newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Caltex delays expansion in troubled Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Caltex delays expansion in troubled Cambodia.

text.p: Caltex Cambodia Ltd officials said on Tuesday they were delaying plans to expand their retail petrol station business in Cambodia in the wake of recent turmoil in the country.

But the officials from Caltex, the largest U.S. investor in Cambodia, said they would press ahead with plans to complete their largest project, an $8 million international marine terminal in the southern port city of Sihanoukville, by early next year.
"We're proceeding with construction there and will finish early next year," manager of operations and logistics Gulam Razzak said at a news conference.
"But we are reviewing the situation at the moment. We want a clearer picture from the government about its new policies...and the government is only one week old," he said.
Caltex had planned to add eight petrol stations by the end of the year but would now only add three or four which were already under construction, Razzak said.

Caltex now has 12 stations in Cambodia and has injected a total of $20 million in the country, including setting up a supply and distribution system, building stations and constructing the marine terminal.
The company officials said two days of fighting in Phnom Penh on July 5-6 and a subsequent day of looting had caused roughly $700,000 in damage to two petrol stations.

Caltex's first retail station, built in June 1996, was completely destroyed by looting. Even the petrol pumps were stolen. At another station, a new food market was cleaned out, said Hong Setha, manager of network development.

Caltex's Phnom Penh petrol stations were operating only during daylight hours because of security concerns. Four expatriate staff have left the country and would return if the security situation improved, he said.

The company had war insurance and was looking into how much of its losses would be covered, officials said. The government has also indicated it may offer some compensation for the looting, they said.
Distribution was running normally, Razzak said. The
company's Dallas and Singapore offices were in contact with the U.S. government concerning the Cambodian situation, Razzak said, but declined to comment further.
Caltex, a 50-50 joint venture between the U.S. multinationals Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc, restarted operations in Cambodia in June 1996 after an absence of 20 years.
